title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
statement: Given a string s of uppercase English letters and an integer k, you may change at most k characters to any other uppercase letter. Return the length of the longest substring that can be made to consist of a single repeated character.
realWorld: Error-budget windows. Given a per-minute stream of health checks, 'what is the longest stretch I can call healthy if I am allowed to excuse at most k blips?' is this problem with two symbols. The same counting shows up in sequence alignment, where you look for the longest region matching a consensus base with at most k mismatches.

examples.explanation: Change both A's to B (or both B's to A). The whole string qualifies: length 4, most common count 2, so 4 - 2 = 2 replacements, exactly the budget.

"AABA" at indices 0..3 has three A's and one B, so one replacement makes it "AAAA". "BABB" at 2..5 works equally well. Length 5 is impossible: every 5-character window here needs at least two changes, which is why the greedy window grows to 5 and is then forced to shrink.
With no budget, every valid window is already uniform. The answer is 1, not 0 — a single character is a valid substring, and this is where a `best` initialised badly shows up.

constraints: s consists of uppercase English letters only

bruteForce.idea: For every start index, extend to every end index, count the characters in that substring, and check whether length minus the most common count is within k.
code: for (int j = i; j < s.length(); j++) {
for (int t = i; t <= j; t++) count[s.charAt(t) - 'A']++;
for (int c = 0; c < 26; c++) maxFreq = Math.max(maxFreq, count[c]);
if (j - i + 1 - maxFreq <= k) best = Math.max(best, j - i + 1);
bruteForce.whySlow: The inner recount rebuilds a frequency table that differs from the previous one by a single character. Extending the window from j to j+1 changes exactly one count by exactly one, and the code instead re-reads every character from i to j to learn that. Across the whole run the same character is counted O(n) times. And the outer restart is the same waste one level up: when a window at start i fails, moving to start i+1 discards a table that only needed one decrement.

patternIdentification:
Two signals together: the answer is a *contiguous* stretch, and validity is a property you can maintain incrementally — 'window length minus the count of the most common character' is the number of replacements this window needs, and it changes by a bounded amount when either edge moves. That is the sliding-window template: **valid window, grow greedily, shrink on violation**. Push `right` forward unconditionally, updating the counters; whenever the window becomes invalid, advance `left` until it is valid again; record the best length at every step.

The transferable part is the phrase 'validity is a monotone function of the window'. Here, if a window needs more than k replacements, every window containing it needs at least as many — so shrinking from the left is guaranteed to reach validity and never has to back up. `max-consecutive-ones-iii` is the same template with 'zeros in the window <= k' as the validity test, and `min-window-substring` inverts it (shrink while *valid* to minimise rather than maximise). Once you can state the validity predicate in one sentence, the code writes itself.

optimized.idea:
Keep a 26-slot count array for the current window and a running `maxCount` of the highest frequency seen. A window [left, right] is valid exactly when (right - left + 1) - maxCount <= k, because you keep the most common character and replace everything else. Grow `right` by one each iteration; while the window is invalid, drop characters from the left. Record right - left + 1 as a candidate answer at every position.

`maxCount` is deliberately never decreased when a character leaves. That looks like a bug and is not: `maxCount` records the best frequency ever achieved, so it can only be stale in the upward direction, which makes the validity test slightly permissive — and a window is only recorded as the new best when it is at least as long as the one that set `maxCount`, which was genuinely valid. The answer therefore never exceeds the truth. Recomputing the max over all 26 slots on every step is also correct and costs a constant factor; use that version if the subtlety would slow you down in an interview.

while (right - left + 1 - maxCount > k) {   // replacements needed = length - most common count

complexity.space: O(1) — 26 counters regardless of input size

commonMistakes: Testing validity as `k >= count of characters that are not the most common one` but recomputing the most common character over the *whole string* rather than the window. "AABBBB" with k = 1 then always compares against B's global count of 4 and reports 6 instead of 5 — the symptom is an answer that is too large and grows with the string.

Using `if` instead of `while` to shrink but still reading `best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1)` from a window that may still be invalid. The non-shrinking form of this solution is correct only if you return `s.length() - left` at the end; mixing the two returns a length no valid window ever had, and it passes "ABAB", k = 2 before failing on longer strings.

Initialising `best = 0` and then returning it from an early `return` path for k = 0, or off-by-one on `right - left + 1`. With s = "A" and k = 0 the answer is 1; a solution that reports 0 has forgotten that a one-character substring is already uniform.
